atoms.text: Echolocation is a way for animals to communicate and see through sound. Animals that use echolocation produce many calls quickly in order to locate objects around them. These calls are so high-pitched that humans cannot hear them with their own ears. Animals are able to see with echolocation because of the sound waves from their high-pitched calls. When the sound waves hit an object or animal they bounce back towards the animal that made the calls. This is what allows them to see. Through the sound waves they are able to see where things are.

There are three types of echolocation calls: searching, feeding and social calls. Many animals that use echolocation are nocturnal, meaning they are primarily active at night. This means that they use echolocation primarily to be able to navigate the world at night, and to hunt. Other animals, especially marine animals, use echolocation as social calls to find each other in the vast ocean. Echolocation calls can be used not only to know in which direction an object is, but also to know how close an object is.

Bats, whales and dolphins, for example, all use echolocation. While bats are nocturnal and use echolocation to navigate the world at night and hunt, whales use echolocation for social calls with other whales. Different animals produce different types of echolocation sounds. For example, dolphins and whales make high-pitched clicking sounds, while shrews make high-pitched squeaks, and hedgehogs make high-pitched whistles.
